title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 102: The Kakapo
passageHtml:
READING B2 (BAND 6.0) — BÀI 102

The Kakapo: Rescuing the World's Stranded Parrot

Paragraph 1. New Zealand is well known for its unusual evolutionary history, and few native creatures illustrate this better than the kakapo. Evolving over millions of years on an isolated group of islands completely lacking native land mammals, this nocturnal, forest-dwelling bird gradually lost the biological ability to fly. Instead, it became the heaviest parrot in the world, with fully grown males reaching up to four kilograms. To move through dense southern beech forests, the kakapo developed strong, clawed legs suitable for walking long distances and climbing high into tree canopies. Its short, rounded wings serve purely for balance and parachute-style braking whenever the bird leaps from branches.

Paragraph 2. In a prehistoric ecosystem where the only threats were giant birds of prey hunting by sight—such as the now-extinct Haast's eagle—the kakapo relied on passive survival behaviour. When startled, the parrot freezes in total stillness, depending on its patterned moss-green feathers to blend into the forest floor. For thousands of years, this natural camouflage offered near-complete protection. However, human arrival shattered that ecological balance. First Polynesian settlers, and later European colonists, introduced non-native mammalian predators including stoats, feral cats, and rats. Because mammals hunt mainly by scent rather than sight, the kakapo's habit of freezing, combined with its strong, sweet musky odour, left the bird completely vulnerable to sudden attack.

Paragraph 3. A further barrier to saving the kakapo lies in its highly unusual reproductive cycle. Unlike nearly all other parrots that form monogamous pairs each spring, the kakapo is the only parrot species known to practice lek breeding. In early summer, males gather on traditional hilltops to dig shallow bowl-shaped hollows in the soil. Over several months, they inflate air sacs in their chests to produce low-frequency booming calls that echo for kilometres across mountain ridges to attract females. Even more frustrating for wildlife managers, kakapos do not breed every year; reproduction takes place only every two to four years, strictly timed with the heavy fruiting cycles of native trees such as the rimu, whose calcium-rich fruit feeds the chicks.

Paragraph 4. By 1977, extensive field surveys could locate fewer than two hundred kakapos, nearly all of them aging males surviving in southern Fiordland. An unexpected discovery of a small breeding population on Stewart Island offered a vital second chance. Determined to prevent total extinction, the New Zealand Wildlife Service launched the Kakapo Recovery Programme and carried out an ambitious rescue operation. Teams captured every single surviving bird and evacuated them to remote offshore islands—including Whenua Hou and Anchor Island—that had been completely cleared of introduced mammalian predators.

Paragraph 5. On these predator-free sanctuaries, conservation biologists deployed intensive, technology-driven care. Every individual bird was fitted with a miniature radio transmitter so researchers could track its daily movements and physical condition. Supplemental feeding stations were positioned along forest trails to encourage breeding activity even during years without abundant rimu fruit. Whenever natural nests were at risk, fragile eggs were moved to clinical laboratories for artificial incubation, and teams pioneered the use of drones to transport fresh semen across steep island terrain to fertilise isolated females. Through this sustained effort, the global kakapo population climbed from a historic low of just 51 individuals in 1995 to more than 240 birds today.

groups.title: Questions 7–12
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 2: "giant birds of prey hunting by sight" (săn bằng thị giác) ↔ I (visual).
Đoạn 2: "mammals hunt mainly by scent rather than sight" ↔ A (scent).
Đoạn 3: Không sinh sản hàng năm mà 2–4 năm một lần (bất thường/không đều đặn) ↔ G (irregular).

q7.text: The kakapo uses its rounded wings primarily to help it glide across long distances between trees.

steps: Đoạn 1: Đôi cánh chỉ dùng để giữ thăng bằng và hãm phanh khi nhảy từ cành xuống (purely for balance and parachute-style braking), không phải để lượn đường dài.

q8.text: The strong body smell of the kakapo made it easier for introduced mammals to locate.

steps: Đoạn 2: Thú săn mồi săn bằng mùi, kết hợp mùi cơ thể nồng ngọt của kakapo khiến nó hoàn toàn dễ bị tấn công.

q9.text: Male kakapos build permanent nests in tree canopies to attract females during the summer.

steps: Đoạn 3: Chim đực đào các hố nông trên mặt đất ở đỉnh đồi (dig shallow bowl-shaped hollows in the soil), không làm tổ trên ngọn cây.

q10.text: All surviving kakapos discovered in Fiordland in 1977 were too old to reproduce.

steps: Đoạn 4: Bài chỉ nói nearly all of them aging males (gần như toàn bộ là chim đực già), không khẳng định toàn bộ đều đã quá già không thể sinh sản.

q11.text: Supplemental feeding stations were designed to allow breeding even when rimu fruit was scarce.

steps: Đoạn 5: "Supplemental feeding stations were positioned... to encourage breeding activity even during years without abundant rimu fruit."

q12.text: Drones have completely replaced artificial incubation in the Kakapo Recovery Programme.

steps: Đoạn 5: Cả ấp trứng nhân tạo (artificial incubation) và dùng drone vẫn được sử dụng song song cho các mục đích khác nhau.
